concept.name: Encryption at Rest & in Transit

relationships.description: Connects Encryption at Rest & in Transit to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Encryption in transit protects data moving across untrusted networks via TLS 1.3/mTLS, while encryption at rest protects persisted disks and backups using AES-256-GCM envelope encryption backed by a KMS.
spark.keyTakeaway: Terminate TLS 1.3 everywhere (including internal service-to-service mTLS), use envelope encryption (DEK + KMS KEK) for storage, and separate key-management permissions from data-storage permissions.

concept.whyItMatters: Unencrypted east-west traffic inside a VPC or Kubernetes cluster lets any compromised pod sniff credentials and PII, while unencrypted snapshots or misconfigured S3 buckets turn a single IAM leak or decommissioned drive into a reportable data breach.
whenToUse: All public and internal network traffic (HTTPS, gRPC, database connections, Kafka/Redis replication) using TLS 1.3 or mTLS.
All persistent storage (EBS/NVMe volumes, RDS, S3/GCS, etcd secrets, backups) using KMS-managed envelope encryption.
Multi-tenant SaaS systems requiring cryptographic tenant isolation via per-tenant Customer Managed Keys (CMKs).
whenNotToUse: Relying solely on disk-level encryption at rest (e.g., AWS EBS encryption) to protect against SQL injection or compromised application IAM roles—authorized read paths decrypt transparently.
Replacing password hashing (`Argon2id` / `bcrypt`) with reversible encryption—passwords must be hashed, never encrypted.
Skipping TLS on internal VPC traffic under the assumption that 'the private network is safe' (violates Zero Trust and compliance frameworks like PCI-DSS 4.0 / SOC 2).
keyPoints: **Encryption in transit** uses TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) with ephemeral ECDHE key exchange (Perfect Forward Secrecy) and AEAD ciphers (`TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384` or `CHACHA20_POLY1305`), ensuring past captures cannot be decrypted even if a server's private key leaks later.
**mTLS (Mutual TLS)** authenticates both client and server via X.509 certificates (e.g., SPIFFE/SPIRE or Istio service mesh), preventing lateral movement inside clusters.

**Envelope encryption** encrypts large payloads locally with a fast symmetric **Data Encryption Key (DEK)** (`AES-256-GCM`), then encrypts the DEK with a **Key Encryption Key (KEK)** held inside a hardware-backed KMS/HSM.

**Storage-layer encryption** (EBS, S3 SSE-KMS) protects against physical disk theft and snapshot leaks, whereas **application-layer (field-level) encryption** protects sensitive columns (SSN, OAuth tokens) even from DBAs and `SELECT *` dumps.
AEAD ciphers (`AES-256-GCM`) provide both confidentiality and integrity/authenticity tags—never reuse a 96-bit nonce/IV with the same key, as nonce reuse breaks GCM completely.

examples.title: Application-level envelope encryption for OAuth refresh tokens
examples.scenario: A SaaS integration service stored third-party OAuth refresh tokens in Postgres. Even with RDS disk encryption enabled, any DBA or read-replica analytics pipeline could read plaintext tokens.
examples.outcome: Implementing envelope encryption—generating a fresh 256-bit DEK per record via `AES-256-GCM`, wrapping it with AWS KMS (`kms:Encrypt`), and granting `kms:Decrypt` only to the auth microservice—blocked unauthorized reads across DB backups and BI replicas.

examples.title: Eliminating TLS 1.0/1.1 & plaintext east-west DB traffic
examples.scenario: A security audit flagged plaintext PostgreSQL connections inside Kubernetes and legacy TLS 1.1 support on an edge ALB.
examples.outcome: Enforcing `TLSv1.3` on the ALB, `sslmode=verify-full` with RDS CA bundles on Postgres clients, and Istio `STRICT` mTLS across namespaces secured all east-west traffic with `<1.2 ms` p99 handshake overhead via TLS session resumption.

tradeOffs.factor: Storage-layer encryption (SSE-KMS / TDE) vs Application-layer field encryption
tradeOffs.pro: Storage-layer encryption is transparent to SQL queries, indexes, and ORMs with near-zero developer effort.
tradeOffs.con: Application-layer encryption protects against DBA/SQLi exposure, but disables range queries (`>`/`<`), sorting, and substring `LIKE` indexes on encrypted columns.

tradeOffs.factor: KMS per-request calls vs local DEK caching
tradeOffs.pro: Calling KMS for every decrypt enforces real-time key revocation and CloudTrail auditability.
tradeOffs.con: Unbounded KMS calls hit API rate limits (e.g., 5,500–30,000 req/s) and add 5–15 ms latency per call; caching DEKs in memory with a short TTL (e.g., 5 minutes) via AWS Encryption SDK solves both.

tradeOffs.pro: mTLS enforces cryptographic workload identity and prevents packet sniffing inside compromised VPC subnets.
tradeOffs.con: Adds automated X.509 certificate rotation complexity (cert-manager/SPIRE) and breaks legacy TCP health checks if misconfigured.

failureModes.name: AES-GCM nonce/IV reuse
failureModes.description: Hardcoding a static IV or using a weak counter across restarts with the same AES-256-GCM key allows an attacker to XOR ciphertexts and forge authentication tags.
failureModes.mitigation: Always generate a cryptographically random 96-bit nonce (`os.urandom(12)`) per encryption call, or rotate DEKs well before `2^32` messages.

failureModes.name: Expired or unverified TLS certificates (`sslmode=require` trap)
failureModes.description: Using `sslmode=require` (instead of `verify-full`) or `InsecureSkipVerify: true` encrypts the wire but skips hostname/CA validation, leaving connections open to MitM.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce `verify-full` with pinned CA bundles and automate short-lived certificate rotation (e.g., 24-hour SPIFFE certs or Let's Encrypt) with expiry alerts at 14 days.

failureModes.name: Co-located key and ciphertext
failureModes.description: Storing a hardcoded AES key in `.env` or the same database/S3 bucket as the encrypted backups renders encryption useless on a bucket leak.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep KEKs strictly inside KMS/HSM; grant the backup/storage role `s3:GetObject` without `kms:Decrypt`.

failureModes.name: Unencrypted swap, logs, and core dumps
failureModes.description: Decrypted PII or DEKs written to stdout logs, APM traces, or unencrypted `/tmp` swap files leak outside the encrypted database.
failureModes.mitigation: Scrub sensitive fields before logging, disable swap on app nodes, and encrypt ephemeral NVMe/root volumes.

commonMistakes: Using `AES-ECB` (which leaks patterns) or unauthenticated `AES-CBC` without HMAC (vulnerable to padding oracle attacks) instead of `AES-256-GCM`.
Assuming `HTTPS` at the load balancer means internal traffic to microservices and databases is encrypted.
Leaving `TLS 1.0`/`1.1` or weak RSA key-exchange ciphers enabled for 'backward compatibility'.
Using `sslmode=require` in PostgreSQL/MySQL drivers and thinking it prevents Man-in-the-Middle attacks (it does not verify the server certificate CN/SAN).
Encrypting user passwords instead of hashing them with `Argon2id` + per-user random salt.

sections.content:
## The idea

Data lives in two vulnerable states: moving across a network (**in transit**) and sitting on disk, snapshots, or object storage (**at rest**). Protecting both requires two distinct cryptographic architectures.

In transit, **TLS 1.3** (and **mTLS** for service-to-service traffic) establishes an authenticated, ephemeral session key via ECDHE so passive sniffers and active MitM attackers see only authenticated ciphertext. At rest, **envelope encryption** pairs fast symmetric **AES-256-GCM** (via a per-object Data Encryption Key, DEK) with a hardware-backed **KMS Key Encryption Key (KEK)**—so keys never sit next to the data they protect.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a client uploading a sensitive tax PDF to a microservice backed by KMS and S3:
1. **In Transit (Edge & Mesh)**: The browser connects via **TLS 1.3** (`TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`) to the API Gateway. Inside the cluster, the Gateway forwards the payload over **mTLS** (mutual X.509 certificates issued by Istio/SPIRE) to the Document Service.
2. **DEK Generation**: The Document Service calls `kms:GenerateDataKey(KeyId=alias/tax-docs, KeySpec=AES_256)`, receiving a 32-byte plaintext DEK and an encrypted DEK blob.
3. **Local AEAD Encryption**: In memory, the service generates a random 96-bit nonce, encrypts the PDF bytes with `AES-256-GCM(DEK, nonce, aad=tenantId)`, and immediately zeros the plaintext DEK after use.
4. **Persistence**: It writes `{ ciphertext, nonce, encryptedDEK, keyVersion }` to S3 (which also applies storage-layer SSE-KMS).
5. **Separation of Duties**: A backup auditor with `s3:GetObject` but without `kms:Decrypt` cannot read the PDF.

sections.content:
## TLS 1.3 & mTLS internals

**TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)** removes legacy, broken primitives (RSA key transport, CBC, SHA-1, RC4) and cuts the handshake to **1-RTT** (`ClientHello` + `key_share` -> `ServerHello` + encrypted `Certificate`/`Finished`). Every connection uses ephemeral ECDHE, guaranteeing **Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS)**.

For internal microservices, **mTLS** requires the client to also present a valid X.509 certificate during the handshake. Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) automate 24-hour certificate rotation via SPIFFE IDs (`spiffe://cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/payments`), eliminating static API keys between services.

## Encryption layers & threat model comparison

| Layer | Mechanism | Protects Against | Does NOT Protect Against |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Edge & Mesh Transit | TLS 1.3 / mTLS (`ECDHE` + `AES-GCM`) | Wi-Fi/ISP sniffing, BGP hijacks, pod-level MitM | Compromised application memory or SSRF |
| Disk / Volume At Rest | EBS / LUKS (`AES-XTS-256`) | Physical drive theft, decommissioned hardware | Snapshot sharing with same KMS key, SQLi |
| Object / DB TDE | S3 SSE-KMS, RDS KMS | Leaked raw DB files or backup buckets | Authorized app IAM role or DBA `SELECT *` |
| App-Layer Envelope | `AES-256-GCM` + KMS KEK + AAD | DBA snooping, BI replica leaks, cross-tenant swaps | Compromised app runtime with `kms:Decrypt` |

## Failure modes

1. **GCM nonce collision**: Reusing a 96-bit nonce with the same DEK leaks the XOR of two plaintexts and allows key-recovery of the GHASH authentication key.
2. **Missing AAD binding**: Omitting Associated Authenticated Data (`tenantId` or `recordId`) lets an attacker with DB write access copy an encrypted ciphertext blob from Tenant A into Tenant B's row (confused deputy attack).
3. **Unchecked cert verification**: Leaving `rejectUnauthorized: false` or `sslmode=require` (without `verify-full`) silently accepts attacker-signed certificates.
4. **KMS outage / throttling**: Calling KMS synchronously on every single DB row read without a bounded local DEK cache causes cascading latency spikes.

## Key rotation & operational hygiene

- Enable **automatic annual KEK rotation** in KMS; KMS retains old key versions transparently for decryption while encrypting all new DEKs under the latest version.
- For application-layer DEKs, rotate on a schedule or after `2^30` encryptions per key, and use **blind indexes** (HMAC-SHA256 with a separate key) if you need exact-match lookups on encrypted PII columns like `email`.
- Audit every `kms:Decrypt` call in CloudTrail/SIEM to detect anomalous bulk data exfiltration.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Enforce `TLSv1.3` (minimum `TLSv1.2`) on all public ALBs/CDNs with HSTS enabled.
- [ ] Enable `STRICT` mTLS across internal service-to-service traffic and `sslmode=verify-full` on all DB clients.
- [ ] Enable KMS-backed encryption at rest on all volumes, databases, queues, and automated backups.
- [ ] Use `AES-256-GCM` with fresh random 96-bit nonces and tenant/record `AAD` for sensitive application fields.
- [ ] Separate storage IAM permissions from `kms:Decrypt` permissions.
- [ ] Monitor certificate expiration (<14 days) and KMS API throttling alarms.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Encryption At Rest Transit

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Encryption in transit protects data moving across untrusted networks via TLS 1.3/mTLS, while encryption at rest protects persisted disks and backups using AES-256-GCM envelope encryption backed by a KMS.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Cloud KMS / HSM applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Encrypted Storage.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Encrypted Storage experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always generate a cryptographically random 96-bit nonce (`os.urandom(12)`) per encryption call, or rotate DEKs well before `2^32` messages.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Terminate TLS 1.3 everywhere (including internal service-to-service mTLS), use envelope encryption (DEK + KMS KEK) for storage, and separate key-management permissions from data-storage permissions.
Avoid trap: Using `AES-ECB` (which leaks patterns) or unauthenticated `AES-CBC` without HMAC (vulnerable to padding oracle attacks) instead of `AES-256-GCM`.
Avoid trap: Assuming `HTTPS` at the load balancer means internal traffic to microservices and databases is encrypted.
When to reach for it: All public and internal network traffic (HTTPS, gRPC, database connections, Kafka/Redis replication) using TLS 1.3 or mTLS.
When to reach for it: All persistent storage (EBS/NVMe volumes, RDS, S3/GCS, etcd secrets, backups) using KMS-managed envelope encryption.

putItTogether.title: Putting Encryption At Rest Transit Together
putItTogether.summary: Terminate TLS 1.3 everywhere (including internal service-to-service mTLS), use envelope encryption (DEK + KMS KEK) for storage, and separate key-management permissions from data-storage permissions.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Encryption At Rest Transit before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Implementing envelope encryption—generating a fresh 256-bit DEK per record via `AES-256-GCM`, wrapping it with AWS KMS (`kms:Encrypt`), and granting `kms:Decrypt` only to the auth microservice—blocked unauthorized reads across DB backups and BI replicas.
